extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and comedy writers/producers interested in David Letterman's Top Ten List segment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for producing/structuring a late-night 'Top Ten' comedy list segment, covering topic selection, presentation, pacing, production elements, and adaptions across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous thematic topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The lists were usually given humorous topics such as 'Top Ten Signs Your Kid Had A Bad First Day At School' or 'Top Ten Rejected James Bond Gadgets'. Each list circulated around a common theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a clear, unified theme that lends itself to multiple punchlines; examples on the page show family/relationship jokes, pop-culture riffs, and parody of genre lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality / current events sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some [Top Ten lists] were based on current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recent news or cultural moments as the hook for relevance and immediacy (the article notes lists tied to events such as the 2012 presidential campaign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of absurd or mundane categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Letterman would also occasionally give an intentionally absurd and mundane category, such as 'Top Ten Numbers Between One and Ten', drawing humor from the silliness of ranking such items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose categories that are inherently silly or trivially constrained to create humor from the premise itself (the joke comes from the absurdity of applying a 'top ten' structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest presenters or multiple presenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Many guests like Adam Sandler or Bill Murray would come into the show to provide the answers. At times, the list has also been given by a series of presenters, with each providing one entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guest voices to vary delivery, create surprise, or leverage celebrity personas for extra laughs (examples include celebrity-stacked final shows and single-guest readings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse countdown order with drum roll accompaniment
rubrics_metrics.description: The entries are read by Letterman in reverse countdown order, and are accompanied by a drum roll performed by CBS Orchestra drummer Anton Fig.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the countdown format and musical cue to build anticipation; rhythm and timing (drum roll + spoken delivery) are part of the gag's architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme-matching montages / background graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six montages: the pyramids, the athletes (usually used for a sports-themed top ten list), the taxi cabs, the water towers, the sewer covers, and, in time for the 2012 presidential campaign, the campaign trail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a montage/visual that reinforces the list's theme; visuals serve as an extra comedic layer and help brand recurring categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Band performance concluding the segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion of the list is then followed by a brief performance by the band, usually a pop song relating to the topic of the list in some way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End the bit with a musical tag that ties back to the joke for payoff and transition to the next segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional twists / format subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally a twist was added, sometimes an alteration of the nature of the list itself. One notable example... the list consisted of only one entry: '#10. There's no way he can improve his image.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break or bend the established rules of the bit (e.g., fewer entries, surprise structure) to generate unexpected laughs; subversion is effective when it contrasts strongly with audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and placement of punchlines (#10, #6, #2 strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer Bill Scheft confirmed... the writers use the three funniest entries on #10 (to start the list strong), #6 (which usually accompanies an on-screen slide change), and #2 (the last opportunity for a laugh before the completion of the bit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute your strongest jokes at positions that maximize perceived momentum (#10 to hook, mid-list beat at #6, and #2 before the wrap); be aware that #1 is traditionally not relied on as the biggest laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic framing via 'home office' locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities that were the supposed source of the Top 10 lists (e.g., Milwaukee, Scottsdale, Tahlequah, Wahoo) served as 'home offices' and a running gag; the home office concept was later phased out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fictional or real locales as a framing device or running gag to add regional humor or continuity, but be prepared to retire bits that stop landing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production-era stylistic elements (animation and graphics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only significant modifications in the Late Show years were the elimination of mentioning a 'home office' and the addition of a computer-animated introduction and closing as well as background graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update visual identity and production values to match the show's era; animation and graphics can refresh a recurring bit while preserving its core structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium adaptation: edit for time and content when repurposing
rubrics_metrics.description: For nearly two decades each Top Ten list was packaged into a nationally syndicated radio feature... The feature was often edited for time, and occasionally edited for content which may have been appropriate for late-night television, but not morning radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting television comedy for other media (e.g., radio), trim for runtime and sanitize or alter content to suit the new audience and broadcasting constraints.
